title: U.S. Open final: Alexander Zverev deflates Ben Shelton and home crowd in one-sided victory
content:
Relive the 2026 U.S. Open men’s final between Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev with live coverage from The Athletic

NEW YORK — Alexander Zverev dashed Ben Shelton’s hopes of making American men’s tennis history Sunday at the U.S. Open. Germany’s Zverev, the No. 1 seed, broke Shelton’s serve in the opening game of the final and then settled into the latest edition of a matchup that he sometimes appears to be conducting in his sleep.

After Zverev had established a two-sets-to-love lead, Shelton roused himself and the crowd by taking the third set. But Zverev sent them back to sleep in the very next game, breaking serve to set up a 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 win.

With it, the 29-year-old secured his second Grand Slam title of 2026 and of his career, holding serve so routinely in the final game that he did not realize that he had won.

He prevailed over Shelton, the 23-year-old No. 8 seed playing in his first Grand Slam final, in a match decided by Shelton’s inability to move Zverev out of his comfort zone, a gulf in their serve effectiveness and Zverev’s greater experience in major finals. The defeat for Shelton extends the 23-year wait for an American man to win a Grand Slam singles title.

The Athletic’s writers, Ava Wallace and Matt Futterman, analyze the final and what it means for tennis.

Just like every player in their first Grand Slam final, Ben Shelton would have wanted to do one thing to start off on Sunday: hold serve.

Unfortunately for Shelton, he didn’t. Just like Taylor Fritz two years ago, when he was trying to become the first American man in more than two decades to win a Grand Slam title, the opening game went the wrong way.

But this wasn’t any loss of serve. This was Shelton and Zverev showing everything that could make this a bad matchup for Shelton, playing a game that hewed so closely to the plot of their head-to-head that it was like they had been asked to follow a script.

It might have even been as simple as one point. Shelton, already down 0-15, had Zverev where he thought he wanted him. The American was running back and forth across the baseline and then coming in. Problem was, Zverev was able to switch into backboard mode, catching up with a Shelton backhand — his weaker side — into his own backhand, and another forehand into his backhand that other players might have struggled with but Zverev is able to hit in his sleep.

This is why Zverev has won 44 or his previous 45 matches against lefties.

Shelton would draw even with an ace and a forehand volley. But on the next point he took aim at Zverev’s backhand again and curled it wide, because that’s what Zverev does to lefty opponents who want to attack his backhand with their forehands. He makes them cut it so fine that they end up shooting at tiny targets and missing on key moments.

After that, Shelton double-faulted. Zverev stood essentially against the back wall, reminding Shelton that his favorite kick serve doesn’t do very much to hurt him. Shelton sent a short second serve into the net.

It was one game. But it was also sort of everything.

— Matt Futterman

One of the reasons that people were so excited about Shelton so early in his career is his ability to make adjustments on the fly even in high-pressure matches. He’s got good tennis IQ, the confidence to make changes and a game that allows for a great amount of flexibility while holding its structure.

Shelton did not just let Zverev stand at the back fence and dictate — he did a lot of things to counter Zverev’s extreme return-position, He took a lot of speed off his serve and hit it close to 100 mph, to get Zverev on the move and off balance.

The kick serve Shelton likes the best also doesn’t work as well against someone as tall as the 6-feet-6 inch German, so Shelton started aiming his serves so that they would slide out the side of the service box and bounce wide, rather than high. He came to the net to try and make Zverev move up.

The problem with all of these tactics is they’re taxing moves that require a lot of precision over the course of a best-of-five match on a hot, humid day against someone who can turn into a wall when he wants. The problem with one of them — the coming forward — is that Shelton’s volleys and touch shots are still raw and under-developed.

The American was making good decisions and still lost the first set. That revealed the size of the task in front of him in his first major final.

— Ava Wallace

If one were to assemble a list of best servers on the men’s tour, Shelton and Zverev would be up at the top. But in this specific matchup, everything Zverev does that gets under Shelton’s skin also defangs his biggest weapon.

By the time Shelton went two sets down against Zverev, he hadn’t created a break point.

At the end of the second set, Shelton was serving just slightly better, making 70 percent of his first serves to Zverev’s 68 percent. But the different in points won off of first serves told the story: Shelton was winning 70 percent of first-serve points compared to Zverev’s 93 percent. Shelton is generally a more accurate server than Zverev, but the German’s deep return position was neutralizing a lot of the advantage Shelton could have hoped for.

Two more holds for Zverev later, and Shelton hadn’t broken the German’s serve in 63 service games. The issue for Shelton in this match is Zverev is getting at his serve fairly effectively and Shelton can’t find his way into Zverev’s serve at all. He’s played two sets without manufacturing a break point.

Returning has long been one of the larger vulnerabilities in Shelton’s game, but he’s done a good job addressing that during the summer hard-court swing. What he’s doing just isn’t working against Zverev — especially since Shelton’s forehand went a bit wonky on him in the second set — who has more experience in five-set matches and, despite that he was also playing for a Grand Slam title, wasn’t under 23 years of pressure.

Zverev spent the afternoon playing like he had all the time in the world, drawing errors out of Shelton while simply holding strong on serve. When Shelton finally recorded a break point after two hours and 18 minutes, Zverev crunched a backhand crosscourt to dismiss the opportunity.

That’s not an easy thing to do, but playing conservatively is a smart move in a matchup that does not present too many real problems.

— Ava Wallace

Great players find a way to win when they don’t have their best tennis. They hang around, hunt for an opening and then jump on it when the slightest one arises.

Thats what Shelton needed to do on a day when Zverev wasn’t giving him much and he wasn’t giving himself much either. Still, there were openings, because Shelton was figuring out the patterns he needed to play as the match unfurled. If only Shelton could have executed on them the way he did against Carlos Alcaraz and Frances Tiafoe in the previous two rounds.

At 3-3, 30-30 on Zverev’s serve in the second set, the window opened. Shelton worked Zverev around, and had a shortish forehand bouncing high. He cocked his arm and prepared to pounce. He took hit inside-out into Zverev’s forehand … But missed it long.

Two points later, another forehand, this one a little deeper, but the ball again floating into his strike zone. Long again.

Then it was 5-5, again with Zverev serving and Shelton looking to make the German feel some tension.

Shelton earned a short ball that he could slice deep down the line, pinning Zverev in the back corner. He floated that long, too.

For much of the afternoon, Shelton executed decently on his patterns when he was behind, keeping himself alive and giving himself chances, but not when he was even or ahead and he needed to put Zverev on the back foot.

On to the tiebreak they went. Shelton needed to get ahead quickly. In a flash, it was Zverev who was up 5-0. The set was gone.

— Matt Futterman

If Shelton was going to have any chance, he was going to have to use his serve to start exerting scoreboard pressure.

He was getting almost nothing on Zverev’s serve, so the only thing he could do was use his own as far as it could take him. That’s about how it all went in a third set that didn’t turn until the 12th game, when Shelton finally broke through as the pressure mounted on Zverev’s being either a handful of points, or at least one more set, away from the title.

Shelton had to get there first though. And he did by dominating Zverev on his own serve. He won 19 of 21 points on his first serve and five of seven on his second serve.

Playing from behind, Zverev finally buckled, playing his worst game of the afternoon as he tried to serve the match into a tiebreak.

Shelton responded to winning the set on a missed forehand volley from Zverev by putting a finger to his ear to ask the crowd for noise and raising both eyebrows, as if to say, “Were you all counting me out?”

The American’s body language had been generally positive throughout the match, but his demeanor after finally breaking Zverev’s serve for the first time in 67 consecutive service games was jubilant. It was as if he hadn’t already been on a tennis court for nearly three hours.

Then, all that momentum swung right back in Zverev’s direction in the first game of the fourth set. At 30-30, Zverev caught Shelton at net with a volley into his body, and Zverev hit his next shot for an easy winner. Shelton saved one break point to send it to deuce, but he gave Zverev another opportunity when his inside-out forehand, a shot that had worked well throughout the match, just missed the line wide.

If Zverev hadn’t already reclaimed the match’s momentum, the next point killed any rhythm Shelton had going. The American tried to hang with Zverev in a 24-shot rally, but he finally carried a backhand wide to lose the game, and with it, any realistic chance of a comeback.

— Ava Wallace and Matt Futterman

When he held a two-set lead, it fel as if Zverev could settle into a true comfort zone. Really, he’d been in that zone all afternoon.

That’s not so much of a surprise given how much experience he has on stages like this compared to Shelton. He was so nervous in his first Grand Slam final that he lost a two-set lead to Dominic Thiem at this tournament six years ago, in a match that devolved into a slice-fest of soft serves until Thiem, the Austrian who retired in 2024, seized control with some ripping groundstrokes and won the match.

He was far better the next time around, at the 2024 French Open, when he lost to Carlos Alcaraz in five sets. Jannik Sinner was too good at the 2025 Australian Open. It wasn’t until the French Open final this year, when Zverev played a debutant, Flavio Cobolli, that he held it together at the end of a tournament.

Shelton was another debutant Sunday, with a lot of learning opportunities in front of him that Zverev had already studied. Plenty of players lose one major final — or in Zverev’s case, three — before they win one.

Shelton never seemed truly at ease the way he had in the semis and the quarters on Sunday, especially in the first set. That’s the only set where he lost his serve.

By the third set he’d found something close to stable footing, but by then it was too late and the margin for error too small, as the start of the fourth set proved.

— Matt Futterman
